Both statements are true, and the dimensional identity is precisely why the first one
holds.
**Step 1 — find the dimensions of Planck's constant.** From E = hν:
[h] = [E]/[ν]
= [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹]
= **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 2 — find the dimensions of angular momentum.** From L = mvr:
[L] = [M][L T⁻¹][L]
= **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.** They are identical, so the assertion that h **represents** angular
momentum is sound, and the reason states exactly the ground for it ✓
**Step 4 — match to the options.** Both true, and the reason is the correct explanation ✓
**Why this is more than a coincidence.** Planck's constant is literally the **quantum of
angular momentum** ✓ In the Bohr model the electron's angular momentum is quantised as
L = nh/2π = n ℏ
and in quantum mechanics every angular momentum - orbital or spin - comes in multiples
or half-multiples of **ℏ**. The electron's spin is ℏ/2.
**The unit, read two ways.** The joule-second (J s) of Planck's constant is the same as
the kg m² s⁻¹ of angular momentum ✓
J s = (kg m² s⁻²)(s) = **kg m² s⁻¹** ✓
**The numerical value.** h = 6·626 x 10⁻³⁴ J s, so ℏ = h/2π = **1·055 x 10⁻³⁴ J s** ✓
That is the natural unit of angular momentum in the atomic world, and its extreme
smallness is why quantisation is invisible in everyday rotation.
**A caution about dimensional identity.** Sharing dimensions does not always mean sharing
physical meaning - **work and torque** are the standard counterexample ✓ Here, though,
the identification is genuine and is confirmed by the physics, not merely by the
dimensions.
∴ A.

Both statements are true, and the formula quoted is exactly what fixes the unit.
**Step 1 — look at Bohr's formula.**
ν̄ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
where ν̄ is the **wave number** - the number of waves per unit length, ν̄ = 1/λ.
**Step 2 — find the units of each side.**
ν̄ = 1/λ, so its unit is **m⁻¹** ✓
the bracket (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) is a **pure number**, since n₁ and n₂ are integers ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** For the equation to balance, R must carry the whole unit of the
left side:
**R is in m⁻¹** ✓
**Step 4 — match to the options.** Both statements are true, and the second gives the
reason for the first ✓
**The value of the constant.**
R = **1·097 x 10⁷ m⁻¹** ✓
so the longest line of the Lyman series, with n₁ = 1 and n₂ = 2, has
ν̄ = 1·097 x 10⁷(1 − ¼) = 8·23 x 10⁶ m⁻¹, giving λ = **121·6 nm** - the known
ultraviolet wavelength, which confirms both the value and the unit.
**Why "wave number" rather than "wavelength".** Working in 1/λ turns the hydrogen
spectrum into a simple **difference of two terms**, which is what made the pattern
visible to Balmer and Rydberg in the first place ✓ The reciprocal unit is the price of
that simplicity.
**A caution about the symbol R.** The same letter is used for the **gas constant**
(8·314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) and for **resistance** ✓ They are unrelated; context and units
distinguish them, and the m⁻¹ here is the signature of the Rydberg constant.
**An alternative form.** Some texts write R in energy units, R_E = **13·6 eV**, the
ionisation energy of hydrogen ✓ The two are related by R_E = hcR, which is itself a good
dimensional check: [J s][m s⁻¹][m⁻¹] = **J** ✓
∴ A.

Both statements are true, and the second explains the first exactly.
**Step 1 — recall the formula.**
s_n = u + (a/2)(2n − 1)
This is the distance travelled during the **nth second** of the motion.
**Step 2 — check its dimensions.** Every term on the right is a **velocity**:
u: **[L T⁻¹]**
(a/2)(2n − 1): [L T⁻²] times a pure number = **[L T⁻¹]** ✓
So s_n has the dimensions of **velocity**, [L T⁻¹], and the first statement is **true**.
**Step 3 — see why.** s_n is a distance divided, in effect, by a time interval of
**one second** ✓ Numerically the one disappears, but dimensionally it does not: the
quantity is a distance per unit time, which is a velocity. That is precisely what the
second statement says.
**Step 4 — match to the options.** Both true, and the second is the correct explanation ✓
**The apparent paradox, resolved.** s_n is measured in **metres**, yet its dimensional
formula is that of a velocity ✓ The resolution is that the formula carries a hidden
factor of "per second", with the numerical value 1, which affects the dimensions but not
the number.
**Writing it honestly.** The unambiguous form is
s_n = u(1 s) + (a/2)(2n − 1)(1 s)
restoring the time factor ✓ With that written in, both sides are plainly lengths, and
the dimensional puzzle disappears.
**A worked instance.** With u = 10 m s⁻¹ and a = 2 m s⁻², the fifth second gives
s₅ = 10 + 1(9) = **19**, that is **19 m** ✓ while the formula's terms are velocities in
m s⁻¹ - the numbers agree because the interval is exactly one second.
**Why this matters in examinations.** Dimensional analysis will **not** detect an error
in a formula of this kind, because the hidden unit factor breaks the usual rules ✓
Knowing where such factors lurk is part of using dimensions safely.
∴ A.

Set the gain in potential energy equal to the kinetic energy and solve for the height.
**Step 1 — write the two energies.**
kinetic energy: **½mv²**
potential energy gained in rising h: **mgh**
**Step 2 — equate them.**
mgh = ½mv²
**Step 3 — cancel the mass.**
gh = ½v²
**h = v²/(2g)** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
h = (30)²/(2 x 10)
= 900/20
= **45 m** ✓
**Why the mass cancels.** Both energies are proportional to m ✓ so the answer is the same
for a pebble and for a boulder - a heavy body needs more energy, but it also has more to
begin with.
**The physical meaning of this height.** 45 m is exactly the height to which a body
thrown **straight up** at 30 m s⁻¹ would rise ✓ At that point all its kinetic energy has
become potential energy, which is the same condition the question states.
**A check by the kinematic route.**
v² = u² − 2gh
0 = 900 − 2(10)h
**h = 45 m** ✓ the same answer from the equations of motion, with no energy argument at
all - a useful confirmation.
**A sense of scale.** 45 m is about the height of a **fifteen-storey building** ✓ which
shows how much energy a speed of 30 m s⁻¹ - roughly 108 km/h - represents.
**Reading the distractors.** **30 m** ✗ comes from h = v²/(2g) misapplied, or from
reading the speed as the answer. **60 m** ✗ uses v²/g, forgetting the factor of 2.
**20 m** ✗ matches no combination ✓
**The relation to remember.** **h = v²/2g** connects any speed with the height it is
worth, and it is the single most reused formula in mechanics ✓
∴ 45 m.

**Momentum** is conserved in every collision; **kinetic energy** is not.
**Step 1 — why momentum is always conserved.** During a collision the two bodies exert
equal and opposite forces on each other for the same length of time ✓ By Newton's third
law the impulses are equal and opposite, so the momentum lost by one is exactly the
momentum gained by the other. With no **external** force acting during the brief
collision, the total momentum of the system is unchanged.
**Step 2 — why kinetic energy is not.** Energy as a whole is always conserved, but
**kinetic** energy need not be ✓ In most collisions some of it becomes
**heat** - the bodies warm up
**sound** - the bang
**deformation** - a permanently dented or broken body
Only in a **perfectly elastic** collision does none of this happen and the kinetic energy
come out unchanged.
**Step 3 — classify the cases.**
**elastic**: momentum conserved ✓ kinetic energy conserved ✓ (gas molecules, billiard
balls to a good approximation)
**inelastic**: momentum conserved ✓ kinetic energy **lost** ✗ (most real collisions)
**perfectly inelastic**: momentum conserved ✓ kinetic energy loss is a **maximum**, the
bodies moving off together ✗
In every row, momentum is conserved ✓
**A worked instance.** Two 1 kg bodies, one at 10 m s⁻¹ and one at rest, stick together:
momentum: 10 before, (2)(5) = **10** after ✓ conserved
kinetic energy: 50 J before, ½(2)(25) = **25 J** after ✗ half of it gone
**Why momentum survives even when energy does not.** Momentum is tied to Newton's third
law, which holds whatever the bodies are made of ✓ Kinetic energy depends on **how** the
bodies deform, which varies from case to case.
**Reading the distractors.** **Kinetic energy is always conserved** ✗ and **both** ✗ fail
on the worked instance above. **Neither** ✗ denies the one conservation law that always
holds ✓
∴ linear momentum is always conserved.
